Behavior review: jshelperdependenceny, BusyBox quoting test, Python loader

Verdicts and source analysis

87a295d2218859e5aafca0bd1239256d822469ff58b5037e6616e72b21f124c3
jshelperdependenceny@99.0.0: BENIGN, a limited dependency-confusion lab.
All four tar members were inspected. index.js exports date formatting,
character stripping and random-ID helpers. package.json has no dependencies;
preinstall runs node preinstall.js with a shell fallback that ignores failure.
The preinstall logs an overt dependency-confusion/training banner and serializes
package identity, hostname, OS platform, architecture and timestamp. URL scheme
selects http/https; POST writes that JSON and ends the request. The response is
only used for status logging. There is no shell launch from JS, credential/file
read, environment dump, downloaded-code activation or persistence. The only
environment read configures the callback URL; localhost:5656/exfil is the default.
An installer may override it with DC_CALLBACK_URL. This is a real host-reporting
capability, preserved as notable; a configured external recipient and actual
installation authorization are unknown. The README's banner-only/no-env claims
are inaccurate, and its package-name suffix differs from the manifest. Neither
those claims nor the self-described training provenance were accepted as proof
of safety: the restricted executed code and local default tip the verdict.

Forager fetched webhook.site, which is a general webhook/request testing service.
Its root page is not a payload consumed by this package; the example callback
identifier is a placeholder. hackwise.dev failed DNS resolution. Forager attempts
to retrieve the default loopback endpoint repeatedly got connection refused;
retries were stopped after establishing there was no listener here. No dependency
artifacts are declared. Unverified Hackwise affiliation and a possible overridden
callback are the remaining contextual uncertainties. The public high-version
package, explicit dependency-confusion banner, automatic installation trigger
and genuine host callback explain why external scanners/list maintainers might
flag this lab even though these bytes show no covert third-party theft.

59d5d0d3355ffc79aace8f21471c9c1643b07067d25b9222ef2ca13b9045bfa0
starquoted.tests: BENIGN, BusyBox shell argument-quoting regression test.
The 212-byte sample is byte-identical to
busybox-1.37.0/shell/ash_test/ash-parsing/starquoted.tests in the original upstream
busybox-1.37.0.tar.bz2 (sha256
3311dff32e746499f4df0d5df04d7eb396382d7e108bb9250e7b519b837043a4).
Forager provenance records https://busybox.net/downloads/busybox-1.37.0.tar.bz2;
archive and provenance remain in scratch/triage-bad/shell-upstream/generic.
With no arguments the test replaces itself with THIS_SH and the same test file,
passing 1, abc, and 'd e f'. That prevents recursive restart. Four loops print
quoted $*, $@, and their prefixed/suffixed forms. Running with THIS_SH=/bin/sh
produced exactly the upstream .right output. No network/dependency references or
other effects exist. Preserve the accurate notable variable-command exec trait.
The hostile-source label appears to be a corpus/collection mislabel; its exact
origin is unavailable. No malicious deployment context was assumed.

76ead656ac2871cdc26cfcc870e01181444ec47805e29a9713e85a52e0d46150
stage1.zip: MALICIOUS, Windows Python bytecode-loader stub.
The zip has one complete 2587-byte member, app/update_helper.py. The script:
* Lowercases getpass.getuser() and checks membership against a tuple containing
  sandbox, analyst, cuckoo and ordinary researcher-like usernames; a match exits
  before the remaining main sequence. This is a username check, not a host check.
* Runs hidden PowerShell with NoProfile and ExecutionPolicy Bypass. Command text
  adds Defender exclusions for the running interpreter's directory and pythonw.exe;
  SilentlyContinue hides cmdlet errors. subprocess.run does not require success.
* Runs hidden schtasks /Create /F /TN ... /XML for a non-XML-suffixed file beneath
  TEMP. The XML itself is absent, so the trigger, action, privilege and successful
  registration cannot be established. The source proves a registration attempt.
* Reopens sys.argv[0], seeks to 4096 and supplies the rest to a loader function.
  It reads a cached key beside sys.executable, or counts down 99999999..0, joining
  eight decimal digits to a 24-byte salt, testing a 12-byte-nonce ChaCha20
  keystream against a 21-byte known prefix. A successful candidate is cached.
* Decrypts the blob, passes the resulting bytes to marshal.loads, then execs the
  resulting code under a custom module name. No PE loading is inferred from that
  module name or the comments.
The member ends before offset 4096; there is no appended ciphertext to recover.
With these bytes, no cache means no candidate can match the 21-byte prefix of an
empty stream; with a key cache, deserializing the empty decrypted blob fails.
Defender/task operations precede that failure. On a Windows host their attempted
blinding and durable registration, analyst filtering and key-concealed execution
are enough to tip the verdict without a final payload or observed success.
Privileges, task XML, cached key, final payload and actual deployment are unknown.

Rule changes and coverage

The old npm-install-hook-configurable-host-profile-post required only a preinstall
hook, host-field text and a JSON POST. It established no external destination,
unauthorized transfer, dependency substitution or source-to-body linkage. No exact
consumers or other recorded positives were found for it. Preserve those exact
required observations and original type/platform/package scope under
micro-behaviors/os/package-manager/hook-install::npm-preinstall-host-fields-post,
at notable criticality with a co-occurrence description. Remove unsupported
T1195/T1041/T1082/exfiltration claims; do not add a training-name exclusion.

The GraphQL far-future-version-argument matched ordinary JS version object fields
in index.js and preinstall.js. Require @gl_introduced(version: before the high-major
prefix; rename its description to the supported GitLab-directive claim. The
existing consumer and actual GraphQL technique remain. All exact and ancestor
rule references were inspected. The GitLab destructive future-field control still
fires both existing hostile exploit consumers; the ordinary version field does
not fire GraphQL findings. Also correct the HTTP URL-fallback description: the
matcher accepts localhost, so it cannot assert a remote default.

New evidence-supported observations:
* Decrypt -> marshal.loads -> exec provenance, allowing local variable assignments.
* PowerShell argv with the Python process exclusion bound to its -Command source.
* Counter-derived ChaCha20 candidate keys bound to the tested key and returned
  candidate; wrong-key binding does not match.
* A normalized username, blacklist tuple, iteration variable and membership return
  tied together; ordinary username lists and unused analysis labels do not match.

Distinct hostile composites cover key-search bytecode activation with Defender
exclusion, hidden policy-bypassed Python exclusion alongside decrypted bytecode,
and scheduled-task registration by that admitted loader. Two suspicious traits
cover the analysis-username check and runtime key concealment. Neutral crypto,
execution, HTTP and task primitives remain notable. No chosen file, task, cache,
package or endpoint name gates a new conviction.

Verification and before/after results

comparison.json contains per-member counts, classifier outputs and exact ID diffs.
Root counts are unique inherited traits, not a sum that double-counts members:
  jshelperdependenceny.tgz: hostile 1 -> 0; suspicious 0 -> 0; notable 83 -> 83.
    preinstall.js: H/S 0/0 -> 0/0; notable 58 -> 57.
    index.js: H/S 0/0 -> 0/0; notable 2 -> 1.
    package.json, README.md, registry metadata: no count changes.
    classifier BENIGN -> BENIGN; aggregate p 0.9656978 -> 0.88073933.
  starquoted.tests: hostile 0 -> 0; suspicious 0 -> 0; notable 1 -> 1.
    classifier BENIGN -> BENIGN; p 0.000021755695 unchanged.
  stage1.zip and update_helper.py: hostile 0 -> 3; suspicious 0 -> 2;
    notable 44 -> 47. Classifier BENIGN -> HOSTILE;
    aggregate p 0.9125571 -> 0.9995596.

No supported attack detection was lost. Intentional losses were the unsupported
npm exfiltration conviction and false GraphQL member matches; installation,
HTTP POST, host information and version metadata remain covered. The outside-
batch cb31215afb62... identity-beacon.tgz is byte-identical to the existing
identity-exfiltration fixture; its code encodes host/user identity into a silent
HTTPS query. Its 1 hostile/1 suspicious and classifier probability 0.99942625 are
unchanged. The existing benign defacement-wording archive also remains unchanged.
No remaining rule/classifier disagreement exists for these three samples.

Run python3 testdata/python-bytecode-review/check_cases.py from the repository
root. All 12 controls passed. In particular, wrong-key-search preserves only the
AV hostile result, while no-policy-bypass preserves execution and task results;
the hostile composites are not duplicate aliases. Echoing an exclusion beside an
unrelated PowerShell launch does not match the bound exclusion or hostile rules.
Fixtures are scanned, never executed. The loader fixture is the actual extracted
source; modified variants are explicitly named boundary controls.
